newsitem.title: USA: Alleged fundraising abuses date to 1992 - report.
newsitem.headline: Alleged fundraising abuses date to 1992 - report.

text.p: John Huang, a key figure in alleged Democratic fund-raising abuses in the 1996 elections, funneled illegal foreign contributions to the Democrats as long ago as 1992, Newsweek magazine reported on Sunday.
"The paper trail dates back to Aug. 18, 1992, just a few weeks after Bill Clinton was first nominated for president," the weekly news magazine reported in its latest edition.

Senate investigators have uncovered documents showing that on the day an obscure California real estate company called Hip Hing Holdings made a $50,000 contribution to the Democratic National Committee, a similar amount was wired into the company's U.S. bank account from the Jakarta headquarters of the Lippo Group, Newsweek said.
The magazine said Huang was now "nearly destitute, wracking up legal bills he can't pay." He was also reported to be "very depressed."

Senate hearings on alleged campaign finance abuses are trying to determine, among other things, whether China or other foreign interests sought to influence U.S. foreign policy by making illegal donations to Democrats in the 1996 presidential and congressional campaign.
Born in China in 1945 and raised in Taiwan, Huang became a naturalized U.S. citizen in 1976 and built ties to political and financial powerhouses on both sides of the Pacific.
He was the top representative in Los Angeles for the Lippo Group, an Indonesian financial and real estate conglomerate owned by the Riady family, which is also under campaign finance scrutiny.
Time magazine said on Sunday that Arkansas lawyer Joe Giroir played a more pivotal role in the Lippo Group's quest for influence in Washington than Huang.

Time said the Riady family formed a partnership with Giroir, former managing partner in the Rose Law Firm where first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton worked, to line up U.S. investors for the family's Asian ventures.

The new venture, Arkansas Industrial Development Corp., was financed by a Lippo subsidiary, and Giroir's job, for which he drew a $360,000-a-year salary, included serving as Lippo's unofficial representative to the White House, Time reported in its latest issue.
Time said after securing Lippo as a $3 million investor in his company, Giroir contributed a total of $175,000 to the Democrats.

Time said investigators wanted to know if Giroir pulled any strings to get Huang, then head of Lippo's U.S. operations, a Commerce Department job in July 1994 that gave him access to classified economic data from Asian countries where Lippo has a big stake.
